Pasteurization is a food preservation process that uses mild heat, typically below 100°C, to eliminate pathogens and deactivate spoilage-causing microorganisms and enzymes in packaged foods like milk and juice, thereby extending shelf life. The technique is named for Louis Pasteur, whose 1860s work on wine inspired it, though earlier pioneers like Lazzaro Spallanzani and Nicolas Appert developed foundational thermal preservation methods. The process is crucial for food safety, particularly in milk, where it prevents serious diseases like tuberculosis and brucellosis caused by raw consumption. While traditional heat treatment via exchangers remains common, modern non-thermal methods like high-pressure processing also achieve pasteurization with minimal impact on food quality.
